text: Bogotá, officially known as Bogotá, Distrito Capital and abbreviated as Bogotá, D.C., is the capital and largest city of Colombia, administered as the Capital District and serving as the capital of, though not politically part of, the department of Cundinamarca. It holds the status of a territorial entity of the first order, equivalent to Colombia’s departments, and functions as the main political, economic, administrative, industrial, cultural, aeronautical, technological, scientific, medical, and educational center of the country and northern South America. Founded on 6 August 1538 by Spanish conquistador Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada after a harsh expedition into the Andes that conquered the Muisca, the indigenous inhabitants of the Altiplano, the settlement was initially named Nuestra Señora de la Esperanza (Our Lady of Hope) and later renamed Santa Fe de Bogotá in 1540 by royal decree, after the town of Granada where Jiménez de Quesada grew up. The name Bogotá derives from the Chibcha word Bacatá (or Muyquytá), meaning "walling of the farmland" or "The Lady of the Andes," and corresponds to a neighboring settlement between modern Funza and Cota. The Muisca, who inhabited the Bogotá savanna and the Altiplano Cundiboyacense, had a complex society with a luni-solar calendar, religious beliefs centered on natural phenomena, and a rich culture involving agriculture, salt production, trade, and goldworking. The Muisca population at the time of Spanish arrival was estimated at half a million on the savanna and up to two million across the Confederation, occupying an area of about 25,000 km². Trade with neighboring Chibcha and Cariban-speaking groups, including the Guane, Lache, U'wa, Muzo, and others, was central to their economy, with salt, tropical fruits, coca, cotton, and gold being traded every four days. The Muisca diet included tubers, potatoes, fruits, and maize, which was used to make chicha, a traditional alcoholic beverage still sold in central Bogotá. The Spanish conquest began in 1536 with an expedition led by Jiménez de Quesada, who arrived in Muisca territories on 9 March 1537, with only 162 men remaining. The last zipa, Sagipa, surrendered to the Spanish after the death of Tisquesusa in 1537. The city was formally founded on 6 August 1538 at Chorro de Quevedo, with an official founding ceremony held on 27 April 1539 near Theusaquillo, where a council and officials were appointed. The city was granted the title of Muy Noble y Muy Leal (Very Noble and Loyal) on 17 August 1575 by Philip II. In 1550, the Audiencia of Santafé was established, making it the seat of government for the New Kingdom of Granada, and in 1717, it became the capital of the Viceroyalty of New Granada. After independence, on 7 August 1819, following the Battle of Boyacá, Bogotá became the capital of the independent nation of Gran Colombia, and Simón Bolívar renamed the city Bogotá to honor the Muisca people and symbolize emancipation from the Spanish crown. The city is located on a high plateau in central Colombia, at an average altitude of 2,640 meters (8,660 ft), making it the third highest capital city in the world, and covers 1,587 square kilometers (613 square miles), with a consistently cool climate. It is subdivided into 20 localities and hosts central offices of Colombia’s executive, legislative, and judicial branches, including the Office of the President, Congress of Colombia, Supreme Court of Justice, Constitutional Court, Council of State, and Superior Council of Judicature. Bogotá is the financial and commercial heart of Colombia, hosting the country’s main financial market and leading in foreign direct investment, contributing 24.7% of the nation’s total nominal GDP. El Dorado International Airport, named after the mythical El Dorado, is the largest cargo handler in Latin America and ranks third in passenger volume. The city is home to the largest number of universities and research centers in Colombia and is a major cultural hub with numerous theaters, libraries (including Virgilio Barco, Tintal, Tunal of BibloRed, BLAA, and the National Library), and museums. It ranks 52nd on the Global Cities Index 2014 and is classified as a global city type "Alpha-" by GaWC. The area’s earliest human activity dates to around 12,500 BP, with evidence found in El Abra and Soacha, and the Muisca domesticated guinea pigs as a food source by around 0 AD. The Muisca warrior elite wore feathered crowns from parrots and macaws from eastern Andean regions. The first mayors were Pedro de Arévalo and Jerónimo de Inzar, and the city’s governance included a mayor and a council assisted by a constable and police chief. Political unrest, such as the 1781 Insurrection of the Comuneros, influenced the rise of liberal ideas, and Antonio Nariño, a key figure, translated and clandestinely published the Declaration of the Rights of Men and of the Citizen in 1794, spreading revolutionary thought despite being arrested and exiled. The city’s population grew from 18,161 in 1789 to 30,000 by 1819, distributed across 195 blocks.

Rafael Nariño became a politician in Santafé and became familiar with liberal ideas circulating in Europe. He began organizing clandestine meetings with other intellectuals and politicians to discuss and promote the independence of the American colonies from the Spanish crown. In 1794, Nariño secretly translated and published in Santa Fe the Declaration of the Rights of Men and of the Citizen, and copies of his translation were distributed across the continent, sparking political change. The Spanish government banned the pamphlet, discovered the material, and burned any copies found. Nariño was arrested on 29 August 1794, sentenced to ten years in prison and the confiscation of all his property, and exiled the following year. Those suspected of being part of his intellectual circle were also persecuted, though his ideas spread widely. In 1807, following the French invasion of Spain and the abdication of the House of Bourbon to Joseph Bonaparte, local resistance governments known as Juntas emerged in Spain and the American colonies. The dissolution of the Supreme Central Junta after military defeats led to the formation of local juntas throughout Latin America, which strengthened existing independentist ideas. After a junta was established in Cartagena de Indias on 22 May 1810, the Junta de Santa Fe was formed on 20 July 1810, known as the Colombian Declaration of Independence. The Junta adopted the name "Supreme Junta of the New Kingdom of Granada," initially swearing allegiance to Viceroy Antonio José Amar y Borbón and appointing him president, but he was deposed and arrested five days later. After declaring independence, the juntas attempted to establish a congress of provinces, but failed, leading to military conflicts. Between 1810 and 1816, intense conflict arose between federalist and centralist factions over the structure of the new government, a period known as la Patria Boba. The Province of Santafé became the Free and Independent State of Cundinamarca, which soon engaged in a civil war against other juntas that united to form the United Provinces of New Granada and advocated for a federalist system. After a failed campaign against Quito, General Simón Bolívar led a campaign that resulted in the surrender of Cundinamarca in December 1814. In Spain, the war ended and the monarchy was restored on 11 December 1813. King Ferdinand VII declared the colonial uprisings illegal and sent a large army under General Pablo Morillo to suppress the rebellions and reconquer the colonies, culminating in the capture of Santafé on 6 May 1816. In 1819, Bolívar launched a campaign to liberate New Granada. After a series of battles, including the Battle of Boyacá, the republican army under Bolívar reached Santafé, where he arrived victorious on 10 August 1819. Bolívar renamed the city Bogotá to honor the Muisca people and emphasize emancipation from Spain, making it the capital of Gran Colombia. Between 1819 and 1849, there were no fundamental structural changes from the colonial period. By the mid-19th century, key reforms such as abolition of slavery and freedom in religious, educational, printing, speech, and trade sectors were enacted. During the 1970s, radicalism accelerated reforms and significantly transformed state and social institutions. However, during the second half of the century, the country faced recurring rebellions, state conflicts, and civil wars, with the most severe being the Thousand Days' War from 1899 to 1902. In 1823, a few years after Gran Colombia's formation, the Public Library (now the National Library) was enlarged and modernized with new volumes and improved facilities, and the National Museum was founded—both vital to the new republic’s cultural development. The Central University, the first state school and precursor to the current National University, was founded in 1867 and located in Bogotá. President Rafael Núñez ended federalism in 1886, establishing a centralist republic governed by the constitution (with minor amendments) until 1991. Throughout political and administrative changes, Bogotá remained the capital and primary political center. From a population of 20,000 in 1793, the city grew to approximately 117,000 by 1912, with rapid growth after 1870 driven largely by emigration from the eastern highlands. In the early 20th century, Colombia faced the devastating consequences of the Thousand Days' War (1899–1902) and the loss of Panama. Between 1904 and 1909, the liberal party’s legal status was restored, and President Rafael Reyes worked to establish a national government. Peace and state reorganization boosted economic activity, and Bogotá began significant architectural and urban transformation with increased industrial and artisan production. In 1910, the Industrial Exposition of the Century took place at the Park of Independence, showcasing progress in industry, artisan work, Beaux-Arts design, electricity, and machinery. The period from 1910 to 1930 is known as conservative hegemony. Between 1924 and 1928, hard labor struggles began, including strikes in oil fields and the banana zone, resulting in many deaths. Bogotá had little industry, with production primarily consisting of artisan work in specific areas. Plaza de Bolívar and surrounding areas housed hat stores; at Calle del Comercio (now Carrera Séptima) and Calle Florián (now Carrera Octava), luxurious stores selling imported goods opened; at Pasaje Hernández, tailor shops operated; and between 1870 and 1883, four major banks—Bogotá, Colombia, Popular, and Mortgage Credit—opened. Following the 1928 Banana Massacre and conservative party divisions, Enrique Olaya Herrera took office in 1930. During the 16-year so-called Liberal Republic, reforms occurred in agricultural, social, political, labor, educational, economic, and administrative sectors. Unionism strengthened and education coverage expanded. The celebration of the exposition led to numerous infrastructure projects, new construction, and job creation. In 1948, liberal leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán was assassinated, triggering riots known as El Bogotazo, which destroyed much of Bogotá’s downtown. This violence sparked a decade-long civil conflict known as La Violencia. At the start of the 21st century, Bogotá initiated major changes in its urban space and public transport to support demographic and economic growth, positioning it as a strategic hub for international business in Latin America. Key initiatives included the Plan of Territorial Ordering (POT), designed to guide city development for the next two centuries. A major intervention was in transportation: in 1967, there were 2,679 urban buses transporting an average of 1.63 million passengers daily in a city of about 1 million inhabitants and 80 km². As the city expanded to over five million people and more than 300 km², the car fleet grew to over 20,000 vehicles, traffic complexity increased, pollution rose, and the existing transport system became inefficient. By the end of the 20th century, there was no viable public transport alternative to private vehicles, which further encouraged car use, and the city had low competitiveness in Latin America with poor quality of life for most residents. Mayors Andrés Pastrana (1988–90), Jaime Castro (1992–94), and the first Antanas Mockus (1995–97) proposed solutions to public transport with limited success. During Mockus’s second term, discussions began about establishing a mass transportation system to address mobility issues. Under Mockus’s second administration, Bogotá opened a 'zone of tolerancia' legalizing prostitution in a large part of the Santa Fe neighborhood. Mayor Enrique Peñalosa (first term 1998–2000) prioritized public transport in his development plan "For the Bogotá we Want," including the construction of specialized bus corridors with single-use lanes, stations, bridges, bike paths, and pedestrian access platforms. However, Peñalosa became infamous for his campaign against the poor, stating he preferred seeing robbers on the streets than people selling candies. He served a second term (2016–19). After being elected in 2011, Mayor Gustavo Petro clashed with the conservative establishment over the remunicipalization of the city’s garbage collection system. Inspector General Alejandro Ordoñez deposed Petro for alleged constitutional overreach when he attempted to replace private trash collectors, but Petro was reinstated weeks later after a Bogotá court ruled Ordoñez had overstepped his authority. The TransMilenio system of articulated buses opened its first phase in 2000 and now operates 12 lines. As the population grew, buses became overcrowded, leading to the development of the Bogotá Metro, construction of which began in 2021. The city’s cultural equipment plan produced significant results, including the construction of three large public libraries in different sectors: El Tunal (south, by Suely Vargas), El Tintal (west, by Daniel Bermúdez), and Virgilio Barco Vargas (central, in Simón Bolívar Park, by Rogelio Salmona). These libraries expanded access to resources and serve as hubs for BibloRed, Bogotá’s Public Libraries Network, including the Bogotá Digital Library. Located in areas with wide coverage, easy access by public transport and bike paths, and designed by renowned local architects, these libraries provide open-access spaces for education and cultural development. As of 2019, the city’s business centers included Av. El Dorado Business Corridor, Centro Internacional, Parque de la 93, El Lago, North Point, Calle 100, Santa Barbara Business Center, Zona Industrial Montevideo, and Parque Industrial Zona Franca. Grittier areas in the south and southwest continue to face reputations for drugs and crime, while the north features boutique hotels, corporate offices, and affluent residents in chic entertainment districts like Zona Rosa and Zona G. Protests against police brutality began in Bogotá following the death of Javier Ordóñez in police custody on 9 September 2020. The National Police killed 13 people and injured over 400 in their response. Bogotá is located in the southeastern part of the Bogotá savanna (Sabana de Bogotá) at an average altitude of 2,640 meters (8,660 ft), a high plateau in the Andes known as the Altiplano Cundiboyacense. It is the largest city in the world at its elevation, with no urban area both higher and more populous. In the extreme south, the world’s largest continuous paramo ecosystem, Sumapaz Páramo, is found. The Bogotá River runs NE-SW, forming Tequendama Falls to the south, and tributary rivers create valleys with villages based on agriculture, livestock, and artisanal production. The savanna is bordered by the Eastern Cordillera to the east, with the Eastern Hills (Guadalupe and Monserrate mountains) limiting city growth to the south and north. The western boundary is the Bogotá River, and the Sumapaz Paramo borders the south. Most wetlands in the region disappeared—covering nearly 50,000 hectares in the 1960s, down to 727 hectares by 2019, a 98% loss. Bogotá has a subtropical highland climate (Köppen: Cfb, Trewartha: Cfll) with average temperatures of 14.5°C (58°F), ranging from 6 to 19°C (43 to 66°F) on sunny days and 10 to 18°C (50 to 64°F) on rainy days. Dry months are December, January, July, and August; the warmest month is March (19.7°C/67.5°F); the coolest nights occur in January (7.6°C/45.7°F), with fog occurring 220 days per year. The highest recorded temperature is 30.0°C (86°F), and the lowest is −7.1°C (19°F), both at Guaymaral Airport. Rainy months are April, May, September, October, and November, with overcast days, low clouds, and winds, bringing maximum temperatures of 18°C (64°F) and minimums of 7°C (45°F). From 1539 to 1810, the colonial city of Santafé barely changed its urban layout and culture. After independence (1810–1819), it slowly moved away from colonialism. In 1801, the city had 173 blocks and 21,394 inhabitants, showing slow growth during the 18th century. In the early 19th century, life was marked by a lack of cultural activity and public services and strong Catholic religiosity, which dominated daily life. The city’s urban shape remained unchanged from the 1557 layout, growing in area by adding blocks while preserving the checkerboard pattern with the Plaza as the core. Buildings were low-rise, most with one floor and a few with two. Wealthier families had two-floor homes with balconies; building facades were simple, with no ornamentation, as outdoor activities were limited. Due to poor street conditions and lack of night-time social life, ornaments were used indoors. One of the few outdoor activities was visiting the Plaza.

The urban layout of Bogotá remained largely unchanged from the 16th to the 19th century, maintaining a checkerboard pattern centered on the Plaza, which served as the city’s social and civic core. Buildings were low-rise, with most having one floor and a few no more than two, and the facades were simple, featuring only walls with windows and entry doors, as noted in a traveler’s account from 1830 (Bibliotheca Luis Angel Arango, 1990,2). The few two-floor homes, belonging to the wealthiest families, were distinguished by their balconies. Due to poor street conditions and limited nighttime social activity, ornamental features were primarily used indoors where residents spent most of their time. The only significant outdoor activity was visiting the Plaza, known locally as the "altozano," where people from all socioeconomic backgrounds gathered to buy fresh fruits. After Colombia’s independence, which lasted from 1810 to 1819, gradual changes began as the new republic sought to distance itself from colonial rule by renaming streets, plazas, and the city from Santafé to Bogotá. Colonial street names were replaced with numbers and plazas were renamed after national founding fathers. The Plaza evolved into an ornamented public space with trees and civic statues; the first such statue, of Simón Bolívar, was unveiled on July 20, 1846, coinciding with Colombia’s Independence Day. From 1870 to 1900, Bogotá saw a more defined shift in its urban landscape, driven by rural migration that sustained the city’s regional influence. In 1847, the city governor and council attempted to expand beyond colonial boundaries, a move fully supported only by President Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera from the 1860s. The Mosquera plan included lotting the western area, building bridges, and widening roads and plazas, though only partially implemented. In the following decade, private entrepreneurs proposed infrastructure projects such as sewers, theaters, electric systems, and new roads to accelerate development, though these were delayed by the 1876 civil war. Nevertheless, the council adopted Bogotá’s first urban code in 1875. Development remained slow until 1882, when the arrival of the train and trolley spurred faster progress. Today, Bogotá is divided into 20 localities—Usaquén, Chapinero, Santa Fe, San Cristóbal, Usme, Tunjuelito, Bosa, Kennedy, Fontibón, Engativá, Suba, Barrios Unidos, Teusaquillo, Los Mártires, Antonio Nariño, Puente Aranda, La Candelaria, Rafael Uribe Uribe, Ciudad Bolívar, and Sumapaz—forming a network of neighborhoods. Higher economic status is concentrated in the north, near the Eastern Hills, particularly in Chapinero, Usaquén, and eastern Suba, while the lower middle class lives in the central, western, and northwestern areas, and working-class neighborhoods, including squatter areas, are located in the south. The city’s central layout is based on a plaza-centered design, with Calles running west to east and Carreras running north to south, numbered accordingly with directional suffixes. Addresses are now assigned based on street rank, and major roads have both numbers and proper names. Bogotá has a population of 7,412,566 (2018 census), with a density of approximately 4,310 inhabitants per square kilometer, and 25,166 residents in rural areas of the Capital District; 47.8% are male and 52.2% female. Urbanization has accelerated due to industrialization, poverty, and violence, leading to rural-to-urban migration, with an estimated floating population of up to 4 million, mostly migrant workers and displaced people, concentrated in Ciudad Bolívar, Kennedy, Usme, and Bosa. The city has significantly reduced its crime rate, from 81 murders per 100,000 in 1993 to 14 per 100,000 in 2017, due to the "Comunidad Segura" security policy introduced in 1995. In 2022, 13.28% of births were to foreign mothers. The ethnic composition includes 0.9% Afro-Colombian and 0.3% Indigenous populations, with 98.8% of residents having no ethnic affiliation, mostly White and Mestizo. Bogotá is the capital of Colombia, housing the Congress, Supreme Court, executive center, and the President’s residence (Casa de Nariño), all located near the Plaza de Bolívar in La Candelaria. The Mayor and City Council, both elected by popular vote, manage city administration; Carlos Fernando Galán was elected in 2023, with a term from 2024 to 2027. Each locality is governed by an administrative board of at least seven members, with local mayors appointed by the Mayor from candidates nominated by the board. Bogotá is the main economic and industrial center of Colombia and a key destination for capital goods imports. The metro contributes 38% of Colombia’s GDP (150 billion dollars in 2024), and travel and tourism account for 2.5% of the city’s GDP, with Bogotá responsible for 56% of Colombia’s tourism and hosting 1,423 multinational companies. It is recognized as a global city for business and meetings, having hosted 50 major international events in 2016 and 12 more in progress, including the 16th World Summit of Nobel Peace Laureates in 2017 and the One Young World Summit in 2017. The historical center of La Candelaria offers cultural attractions, museums like the Botero and Gold Museums, and hostels, while Cerro Monserrate is accessible by cable car or funicular. Tourist sites include the José Celestino Mutis Botanical Garden, Quinta de Bolívar, national observatory, planetarium, Maloka, Colpatria, La Calera, monument of American flags, and La Candelaria. Usaquén features a traditional Sunday flea market and brunch. Green areas such as Quebrada La Vieja and Chapinero Waterfalls offer eco-tourism and hiking. Gastronomic areas include the G Zone, T Zone, and La Macarena. Since the 2000s, major hotel chains have established themselves, reflecting the city’s cultural diversity. New shopping malls have boosted the economy; as of 2011, over 160 new malls were planned in addition to 100 existing ones. Bogotá hosts major television stations including Canal Capital, Citytv, Canal 13, Caracol TV, RCN TV, Canal Uno, Canal Institucional, and Señal Colombia, along with satellite services like Telefónica, Claro, and DirecTV. Major radio networks are available in AM and FM, with 70% of FM stations offering RDS. Newspapers include El Tiempo, El Espectador, El Nuevo Siglo, La República, Portafolio, El Espacio, Q'Hubo, and Extra, plus three free papers—ADN, Publimetro, and The Bogotá Post. Energy and sewer bills are stratified by residential property location, not household income, and all mayors are required to conduct such stratification. The city’s social strata are used by the government for welfare programs and land allocation. In addition to TransMilenio, policies such as Pico y Placa (peak-hour license plate restrictions), 121 kilometers of Ciclovía on Sundays and holidays, and a 376-kilometer network of segregated bicycle paths (ciclorrutas), which extends from 170th Street to 27th Street and from Monserrate to the Bogotá River, have been implemented to promote cycling and reduce car use. The ciclorruta, initiated by the 1995–1998 Antanas Mockus administration and expanded through a Bicycle Master Plan, is one of the most extensive dedicated bike path networks globally. Since its creation, bicycle use has increased, and a car-free week was introduced in 2014. The metropolitan area now has over 650 kilometers of urban bicycle paths. Due to rapid urbanization and immigration, downtown congestion has increased, but since the creation of the Bogotá Metropolitan Area in 1990, infrastructure improvements have been made, including new avenues, boulevards, and the first two metro lines. Recent projects include the expansion of Avenida Boyaca and Autopista Norte, and the construction of Avenida Guayacanes, a 13-kilometer, eight-lane avenue in Bosa and Kennedy, as well as excavations for the second metro line. Private car ownership, along with taxis, buses, and commercial vehicles, contributes significantly to traffic. Buses remain the primary mass transit mode, with two systems: the traditional system and the TransMilenio BRT system. The city is currently replacing the TransMilenio fleet with Euro VI-standard CNG and electric buses, aiming to have the largest electric bus fleet outside China. The traditional system operates various bus types through multiple companies.

Efforts to upgrade Bogotá's infrastructure have included the construction of several new avenues and boulevards, as well as the first two lines of the Bogotá Metro. In recent years, the capital has undertaken city building projects such as the expansion of Avenida Boyaca and Autopista Norte, and the construction of the new 13-kilometer, eight-lane Avenida Guayacanes, being built from scratch in the boroughs of Bosa and Kennedy, alongside excavations for the city's second metro line. Private car ownership significantly contributes to traffic congestion, along with taxis, buses, and commercial vehicles. Buses remain the primary mode of mass transit, operating through two systems: the traditional system and the TransMilenio Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system. The city is currently replacing and updating the TransMilenio fleet with Euro VI-standard CNG-powered and electric buses, aiming for Bogotá to have the largest electric bus fleet in the world outside China. The traditional system includes large buses (Ejecutivo and corriente), medium-sized Busetas, and Colectivos (vans or minivans), with all services now operating as corriente since May 2008. Bogotá is a major hub for domestic and international bus routes, with its terminal serving most Colombian cities and being the largest in the country, and offering international services to Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela. The TransMilenio system was established during Enrique Peñalosa's mayoral term as a bus rapid transit solution to compensate for the lack of a subway or rail system, featuring articulated buses on dedicated busways and feeder buses in residential areas. Its main routes include Caracas Avenue, Northern Highway (Autopista Norte), 80th Street, Americas Avenue, Jiménez Avenue, and 30th Avenue (also known as Norte Quito Sur or N.Q.S.), with routes for Suba Avenue and Southern Highway (Autopista Sur) opening in April 2006. The third phase will cover 7th Avenue, 10th Avenue, and 26th Street (Avenida El Dorado), with the system planned to cover the entire city by 2030. Despite its reach, TransMilenio is more expensive than any public transport except taxis, at US$0.80 or 2,300 COP. El Dorado International Airport, located west of downtown in the Fontibón locality with an area of 6.9 km², is the busiest airport in Latin America and Colombia, globally known as The Hub of the Americas. It was ordered by Gustavo Rojas Pinilla (19th President of Colombia) in 1955 to replace Techo Airport. Due to its central location, it serves as a hub for Avianca, Copa Airlines Colombia, and LATAM Colombia, and is served by international airlines including American, Delta, United, Air France, KLM, Turkish Airlines, Edelweiss, Lufthansa, Emirates, Iberia, and Air Canada. With approximately 27 million passengers annually, the airport has increased its responsibilities due to congestion. A secondary airport, CATAM, serves military and police aviation and uses El Dorado’s runways, with plans to relocate to Madrid, a town in Cundinamarca, to allow for El Dorado’s expansion. Guaymaral Airport, located in the northern boundaries of Bogotá, is used primarily for private aviation. In 2024, the City Council approved a megaproject in three phases: the first phase, implemented in the first year, will include a main port, docks, and vessels along the Bogotá River, costing 250 billion pesos, transporting up to 120,000 passengers per day via seven routes, including a 40-minute journey from Suba to Bosa with El Dorado International Airport station in between; the next two phases, also requiring nearly 250 billion pesos, will strengthen the system and increase capacity. This initiative aims to make the Bogotá River a vital transport artery, improving quality of life and promoting balanced, sustainable urban development. Bogotá has limited railway infrastructure, following the collapse of its tram network, though plans to restore rail services continue. The Bogotá Metro has been advanced by two successive governments, with construction beginning in 2020 and opening planned for 2028. Plans to build railways replacing defunct routes have been delayed due to urgent urban transport needs. A tram train line using the former Bogotá Savannah Railway right-of-way, known as RegioTram, is under construction. On 25 December 1884, the first tramway, pulled by mules, connected Plaza de Bolívar to Chapinero, and in 1892, a line from Plaza de Bolívar to La Sabana Station began operating. The tramway initially used wooden rails, which were later replaced with steel imported from Britain; by 1894, the Bogotá–Chapinero line operated with a 20-minute interval. The system expanded to cover most of the city and its suburbs, but was severely damaged during the 1948 Bogotazo riots and closed due to the subsequent civil war, with operations ceasing in 1951 when they were replaced by buses. Most streetcar tracks were paved over, though exposed tracks remain visible in older roads, especially in downtown and La Candelaria, with about 70 years having passed since any vehicles ran on them. Bogotá has the most extensive and comprehensive network of bike paths in Colombia, known as Ciclorrutas de Bogotá, designed and built during the administrations of Mayors Antanas Mockus and Enrique Peñalosa, and is one of the most extensive in the world and the largest in Latin America. The network is integrated with the TransMilenio system, which includes bicycle parking facilities, enabling seamless cycling across the metropolitan area. The city implemented the "Ciclovía" program, closing major highways from 7:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. on Sundays and public holidays, allowing residents to ride bikes and exercise while reducing pollution. During December, the program is extended at night with special events such as fireworks, street theater, and street food. Since 4 April 2016, Carrera 11 has been reduced from four to three car lanes, with a new bike lane inaugurated. The average weekday commute time via public transit is 97 minutes, with 32% of riders spending over two hours daily; the average waiting time at a stop or station is 20 minutes, and 40% of riders wait over 20 minutes daily. The average distance traveled via public transit is 8 kilometers, with 16% of trips exceeding 12 kilometers in one direction. Known as the Athens of South America, Bogotá has a comprehensive educational system, including primary and secondary schools and colleges. Due to constant migration, state-provided free education quotas are often insufficient, and the city has a diverse mix of public and private schools. There are numerous universities, both public and private, including the National University of Colombia, University of the Andes, District University of Bogotá, La Salle University, University of La Sabana, Pontifical Xavierian University, Our Lady of the Rosary University, Universidad Externado de Colombia, Nueva Granada Military University, Central University, El Bosque University, University of America, Sergio Arboleda University, Jorge Tadeo Lozano University, Pilot University of Colombia, Catholic University of Colombia, Saint Thomas Aquinas University, and Universidad Pedagógica Nacional. The city hosts a University City at the National University of Colombia campus in Teusaquillo, the largest campus in Colombia and one of the largest in Latin America. A private school, Chapinero's English Royal School (Colegio Inglaterra Real de Chapinero), operated from 2008 until 2021 when it closed due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Bogotá has numerous cultural venues, including 58 museums, 62 art galleries, 150 libraries, 45 stage theaters, 75 sports and attraction parks, and over 150 national monuments. Notable institutions include BibloRed, the city’s public libraries network, the Luis Ángel Arango Library, which receives over 6 million visitors annually, the Colombian National Museum (dating back to 1823), the Ibero-American Theater Festival (which attracts 2 million attendees with over 450 performances), the Bogotá Philharmonic (the most important symphony orchestra in Colombia with over 100 musicians and 140 performances annually), and the Cristóbal Colón Theater, the country’s oldest opera house, opened in 1892 and home to the National Symphony Orchestra of Colombia. Rock al Parque, an annual open-air rock music festival, draws over 320,000 fans for three days each year with more than 60 band performances, and has led to the creation of other festivals such as Salsa at the Park, Hip Hop at the Park, Ballet at the Park, Opera at the Park, and Jazz at the Park. Kids' Choice Awards Colombia, hosted by Nickelodeon since 2014, features artists like Maluma, Austin Mahone, Carlos Peña, Don Tetto, and Riva. Bogotá has positioned itself as a leader in cultural offerings in South America and is increasingly recognized globally as a hub for the arts. In 2007, the city was awarded Cultural Capital of Ibero-America by the UCCI (Union of Ibero-American Capital Cities), becoming the only city to receive the title twice, after first receiving it in 1991. Bogotá is home to key literary figures of the Spanish-speaking world, including José Asunción Silva (1865–1896), a Modernism pioneer whose work *De sobremesa* is considered outstanding in American literature, and Rafael Pombo (1833–1912), a romanticism poet whose fables are essential to Colombian tradition. The colonial urban morphology and architecture have been preserved since the late 19th century, especially in La Candelaria, the historical center, with two-story colonial houses featuring courtyards, gabled roofs, ceramic tiles, and balconies. Some balconies were enclosed with glass during the Republican period, as seen in the House of Rafael Pombo. "Republican Architecture" dominated from 1830 to 1930, with only limited examples of modern architectural language, such as University City and White City at the National University of Colombia (1936–39), designed by German architect Leopold Rother, with contributions from rationalist architects. Other architectural trends include Art Deco, Expressionism, and Organic Architecture, the latter typified by Bogotan architect Rogelio Salmona. In 2015, BD Bacatá was inaugurated, surpassing the Colpatria Tower to become the tallest building in the city and Colombia, marking the beginning of downtown renovation. In 2007, Bogotá was named World Book Capital by UNESCO, becoming the first Latin American city to receive the honor and the second in the Americas after Montreal. The recognition was due to coordinated programs, a strong library network, and organizations promoting reading. The city is home to BibloRed, which manages 146 small and four large public libraries (Biblioteca Virgilio Barco, Biblioteca El Tintal, Biblioteca El Tunal, and Biblioteca Julio Mario Santodomingo), as well as six branches of the Colsubsidio Family Compensation Fund Library Network and libraries attached to institutions such as the Museo Nacional de Colombia, Bogotá Museum of Modern Art, Alliance Française, and Centro Colombo Americano. Additional libraries include the National Library of Colombia (1777), with over two million volumes and a significant collection of ancient books, and the Luis Ángel Arango Library (1958), with nearly two million volumes and 45,000 m², hosting 10,000 daily visitors; the Library Alfonso Palacio Rudas, located in the north with about 50,000 volumes, and other large libraries such as the Library of Congress (100,000 volumes), Instituto Caro y Cuervo (nearly 200,000 volumes, the largest Latin American library in Philology and Linguistics), the Academy of History, Academy of Language, ICANH, and various university libraries. The city houses the General National Archive, containing about 60 million documents, one of the largest primary historical sources collections in Latin America, and other archives such as the Musical Archive of the Cathedral of Bogotá, the Archdiocesan Archive, the Archive of the Conciliar Seminary of Bogotá, the Archive of the National University of Colombia, and the Archive of the Mint under the Bank of the Republic. As of 2009, the city had 58 museums and 62 art galleries. The National Museum of Colombia has four collections: art, history, archaeology, and ethnography. The Gold Museum, with 35,000 pieces of tumbaga gold and 30,000 objects in ceramic, stone, and textiles, holds the largest pre-Columbian gold collection in the region.

Bogotá is home to a wide range of libraries, including the Library of the Academy of Philology and Linguistics, the Library of the Academy of History, the Library of the Academy of Language, the Library of the Colombian Institute of Anthropology and History (ICANH), and numerous university libraries. The city houses historical records in the General National Archive, which contains about 60 million documents and is one of the largest repositories of primary historical sources in Latin America. Other notable archives include the Musical Archive of the Cathedral of Bogotá (with thousands of books and choral songs from the colonial period), the Archdiocesan Archive, the Archive of the Conciliar Seminary of Bogotá, the Archive of the National University of Colombia, and the Archive of the Mint in Bogotá, under the Bank of the Republic. As of 2009, Bogotá had 58 museums and 62 art galleries. The National Museum of Colombia has four collections: art, history, archaeology, and ethnography. The Gold Museum contains 35,000 pieces of tumbaga gold and 30,000 objects in ceramic, stone, and textiles, representing the largest collection of pre-Columbian gold in the world. The Museo Botero features 123 works by Fernando Botero and 87 by international artists. The Bogotá Museum of Modern Art holds graphic arts, industrial design, and photography. The Museum of Colonial Art showcases an important collection of colonial art from Colombia. Fundación Gilberto Alzate Avendaño hosts performing arts activities and temporary art exhibitions. Among scientific museums are the Archeological Museum – Casa del Marqués de San Jorge, which holds about 30,000 pieces of pre-Columbian art, the Instituto de Ciencias Naturales (UN), one of the four largest natural science museums in Latin America, and the Geological Museum, specializing in geology and paleontology. Historical museums in the city include the Jorge Eliecer Gaitan Museum, the Museum of Independence, the Quinta de Bolívar, the Casa Museo Francisco José de Caldas, the headquarters of Maloka, and the Children's Museum of Bogotá. New museums include the Art Deco and the Museum of Bogotá. The city hosts the Ibero-American Theater Festival, the largest theater festival in the world, and has forty-five theaters, including the Colon Theater, Teatro Mayor Julio Mario Santo Domingo, the National Theater (with two venues), the TPB Hall, the Theater of La Candelaria, the Camarin del Carmen (over 400 years old, formerly a convent), Colsubsidio, the renovated Teatro Jorge Eliécer Gaitán, León de Greiff Auditorium (home of the Bogotá Philharmonic Orchestra), and the Open Air Theater "La Media Torta." Other theater festivals, such as the "Alternative Theater Festival," are also held, keeping the city culturally active year-round. Bogotá hosts the Bogotá Film Festival and numerous theaters showing contemporary and art cinema. The city's international art fair, ArtBo, takes place annually in October, showcasing thousands of works across all art formats, movements, and concepts. The main cultural center is La Candelaria, the historic center, which hosts universities and museums. In 2007, Bogotá was designated the Ibero-American Cultural Capital. Before the Spanish conquest, the indigenous inhabitants practiced the Muisca religion; since the colonial period, the city has been predominantly Roman Catholic, with many churches in the historic center. The city has been the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Bogotá since 22 March 1564, with the Primatial Cathedral of Bogotá as the seat of the Archbishop, located in new buildings in the north of the city. As of 2023, Bogotá has six mosques, including Abou Bakr Al-Siddiq Mosque on Calle 80 and Carrera 30, Estambul Mosque in Chapinero, and Centro de Estudios Al-Qurtubi on Calle 60. There are four synagogues in the city, with the main Ashkenazi Jewish synagogue located on 94th Street. An Eastern Orthodox church and the San Pablo Anglican Cathedral, the mother church of the Episcopal Church in Colombia, are both in Chapinero. The Bogotá Colombia Temple of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is located in the Niza neighborhood. There are four Buddhist centers in the north of the city, and a variety of Protestant churches, including the Bogotá Baptist Chapel, the non-denominational Union Church, and the St. Matthaus Evangelical Lutheran Church, which holds services in German and Spanish for the German-Colombian community. Bogotá has a diverse array of restaurants in sectors such as Parque de la 93, Usaquén, Zona T, The G Zone, La Macarena, La Candelaria, The Parkway, and the International Center, offering international cuisines including Argentinian, Peruvian, Venezuelan, Brazilian, Mexican, American, Arabic, Asian, French, Italian, Russian, and British. Typical dishes include ajiaco, a soup made with chicken, potatoes, corn on the cob, guascas (an herb), served with sour cream, capers, avocado, and rice; tamales, a traditional dish made with a paste of rice, beef, pork or chicken, chickpeas, carrot, and spices, wrapped in plantain leaves and steam-cooked. Popular desserts include figs with arequipe, strawberries with cream, postre de natas, and cuajada con melao. Canelazo is a hot drink from the Altiplano made with aguapanela, cinnamon, and aguardiente; carajillo is a hot beverage made with Colombian coffee (tinto) and aguardiente. The city has numerous parks with facilities for concerts, plays, movies, storytellers, and other events. The District Institute for Recreation and Sport promotes recreation, sports, and park use. Football is a symbol of Bogotá and is widely played; the city has three professional clubs: Santa Fe, Millonarios, and La Equidad. The main stadium is The Campín Stadium (Estadio Nemesio Camacho El Campín), home to Santa Fe and Millonarios, which hosted the 2001 Copa América final between Colombia and Mexico, ending 1–0 in favor of Colombia, securing Colombia's first continental cup. The other soccer venue is the multi-use Techo Metropolitan Stadium, home of La Equidad. Other major venues include the covered Coliseum El Campín, the Simón Bolívar Aquatic Complex, the Sports Palace, the El Salitre Sports Venue (which includes the Luis Carlos Galán Velodrome, hosting the 1995 UCI Track Cycling World Championships), the El Salitre Diamond Ballpark, and the BMX track "Mario Andrés Soto." Bogotá hosted the first Bolivarian Games in 1938, the National Games in 2004 (winning the championship), and was a sub-venue for the Bolivarian Pan American Games. The city is also on the route of the Tour of Colombia. After hosting the 2011 FIFA U-20 World Cup in Colombia, Bogotá became a venue for the 2016 FIFA Futsal World Cup. The flag originated from the 1810 insurgency against colonial authorities, when rebels wore armbands with yellow and red bands—colors of the Spanish flag used for the New Kingdom of Granada. On 9 October 1952, exactly 142 years later, Decree 555 of 1952 officially adopted the patriotic armband as the flag of Bogotá. The flag of Cundinamarca follows the same pattern with a light blue tile representing the Virgin Mary's cape. The flag consists of a yellow band above a red one; yellow symbolizes gold from the earth and virtues such as justice, clemency, benevolence, and "mundane qualities" like nobility, excellence, richness, generosity, splendor, health, steadfastness, joy, and prosperity, as well as long life, eternity, power, and constancy. Red symbolizes charity, bravery, nobility, values, audacity, victory, honor, and furor, which Colombians refer to as the blood of their people. The coat of arms was granted by Emperor Charles V (Charles I of Spain) in Valladolid on 3 December 1548 to the New Kingdom of Granada; it features a black eagle in the center, symbolizing steadfastness and representing the Habsburgs, the ruling Spanish family. The eagle is crowned with gold and holds a red pomegranate within a golden background. The border includes olive branches with nine golden pomegranates on a blue background; the two red pomegranates represent audacity, and the nine golden ones represent the nine states of the New Kingdom of Granada. In 1932, the coat of arms was officially recognized and adopted as the symbol of Bogotá. The city's anthem was written by Pedro Medina Avendaño and composed by Roberto Pineda Duque, officially declared the anthem by Decree 1000 on 31 July 1974 by then Mayor Aníbal Fernandez de Soto. Bogotá is twinned with various cities and is part of the Union of Ibero-American Capital Cities, established on 12 October 1982. It also cooperates with the departments of Amazonas, Antioquia, Arauca, Atlántico, Bolívar, Boyacá, Caldas, Caquetá, Casanare, Cauca, Cesar, Chocó, Córdoba, Cundinamarca, Guainía, Guaviare, Huila, La Guajira, Magdalena, Meta, Nariño, N. Santander, Putumayo, Quindío, Risaralda, San Andrés, Santander, Sucre, Tolima, Valle del Cauca, Vaupés, and Vichada. The capital district is Bogotá.
